lie: I will build a great, great wall on our southern border, and I will have Mexico pay for that wall. Mark my words.
fallacy: Broken Promise / Unfulfilled Commitment — The wall was not fully built and Mexico never paid for any portion of it.

lie: I won the popular vote by a tremendous margin. We had a massive landslide victory in the Electoral College.
fallacy: Falsehood / Fabrication — Hillary Clinton won the popular vote by approximately 2.9 million votes.

lie: I think we've had the largest audience ever to witness an inauguration — period — both in person and around the globe.
fallacy: Exaggeration / False Comparison — Aerial photos and transit data showed attendance was significantly lower than the 2009 inauguration of Barack Obama.

lie: We are also getting rid of the Defense sequester, which is a very, very important thing. … Because of our military spending bill, what was being done, we are going to be doing a lot more than we were doing before.
fallacy: Falsehood — The 2018 budget preserved the Budget Control Act spending caps; no sequester was eliminated.

lie: And the day before, voter fraud — 3 to 5 million people, people that are dead. And I won by a massive, massive margin. They said 3 to 5 million.
fallacy: Baseless Accusation / Straw Man — No credible evidence of 3 to 5 million fraudulent votes has ever been presented; multiple studies found no widespread fraud.

lie: The murder rate in our country is the highest it's been in 45 to 50 years.
fallacy: Falsehood — FBI data showed the U.S. murder rate in 2016 was near historic lows, not at a 45–50 year high.

lie: Obama had his eight years, and he didn't do it. He didn't do it. I don't know why. He talked about it. But he didn't do it.
fallacy: Misrepresentation — The Affordable Care Act was a major legislative achievement of the Obama administration; the claim ignores that record.

lie: Last year, the trade deficit with China was roughly $500 billion. This is not a free trade situation. It's foolish trade. It's stupid trade.
fallacy: Exaggeration — The actual U.S. trade deficit with China in 2017 was approximately $375 billion, not $500 billion.

lie: I never said the repeal and replace of Obamacare would be easy. I said it would be tough — very tough. But we're going to get it done.
fallacy: Falsehood — On multiple occasions Trump said repealing and replacing Obamacare would be easy, including in March 2017 statements.

lie: We have it under control. It's going to be just fine. … It's one person coming in from China, and we have it under control. It's going to be just fine.
fallacy: False Reassurance / Wishful Thinking — The COVID-19 outbreak escalated into a global pandemic that the U.S. was not prepared for.

lie: It is going to disappear. It is disappearing.
fallacy: Wishful Thinking / False Reassurance — COVID-19 did not 'disappear' and continued to spread widely in the following months.

lie: If we didn't catch the case early, and if we didn't do the right things, it would have been a mass death — a mass death like you have never seen in this country.
fallacy: Contradiction — This statement directly contradicts his earlier claims that the virus was 'under control' and 'disappearing.'

lie: The 2020 election was rigged. We won by a landslide. This was a stolen election.
fallacy: Baseless Accusation / Big Lie — Dozens of courts, state election officials, and the Justice Department found no evidence of widespread fraud; Joe Biden won the election.

lie: I am a very stable genius.
fallacy: Self-Serving Bias / Non-Sequitur — An unsupported self-assessment that adds no evidence to refute the underlying questions about his fitness.

lie: I don't take any responsibility at all.
fallacy: Evasion of Responsibility — A commander-in-chief's statement during an escalating public health crisis, contradicting the expected role of leadership.

lie: The Mexican government … they send the bad ones over.
fallacy: Pants on Fire / Fabrication — No evidence shows the Mexican government encourages criminals to cross the border; most illegal immigration is people seeking work, and Mexican immigration had dropped sharply during and after the recession.

lie: Our real unemployment is anywhere from 18 to 20 percent. Don't believe the 5.6. Don't believe it.
fallacy: Falsehood / Exaggeration — The official U-6 underemployment rate was 10.8%; even the most expansive alternative measures could not plausibly exceed 16%, and the actual rate was 5.5%, not 5.6%.

lie: Even our nuclear arsenal doesn't work. It came out recently they have equipment that is 30 years old. They don't know if it worked.
fallacy: Falsehood — Recent lapses in the U.S. nuclear program involved personnel and command-and-control problems, not equipment that 'doesn't work.' The Pentagon and Energy Department annually certify the arsenal as safe, secure, and effective.

lie: Last quarter, it was just announced our gross domestic product … was below zero. Whoever heard of this? It's never below zero.
fallacy: Pants on Fire / Falsehood — GDP growth has been below zero 42 times since 1946; the economy itself is in the trillions of dollars and never near zero.

lie: When was the last time you saw a Chevrolet in Tokyo? It doesn't exist, folks. They beat us all the time.
fallacy: Mostly False / Exaggeration — Chevrolet sold 597 cars in Japan in 2014; the brand exists there, even if sales are small. The U.S.–Japan auto trade imbalance is real, but the absolute claim of nonexistence is false.

lie: Islamic terrorism is eating up large portions of the Middle East. … They just built a hotel in Syria. Can you believe this? They built a hotel.
fallacy: Falsehood — ISIS did not build a hotel; it seized an existing hotel in Iraq and uses it to house commanders, not to attract paying guests.

lie: I write a book called The Art of the Deal, the No. 1 selling business book of all time, at least I think, but I'm pretty sure it is.
fallacy: Falsehood / Self-Aggrandizement — Nielsen BookScan data shows The Art of the Deal has sold roughly 177,000–184,000 copies since 2001, far fewer than multiple other business titles (e.g., The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People, Built to Last, The One Minute Manager).

lie: You have illegal immigrants pouring through the country. … They're incarcerated. Many of them are in jails. You have hundreds of thousands of people going to state and federal penitentiaries. That just came out in a Homeland Security Report.
fallacy: Falsehood / Fabricated Statistic — Homeland Security confirmed it does not regularly track the incarcerated illegal-immigrant population, and no such report exists. Bureau of Justice Statistics data shows roughly 90,000 noncitizens in state and federal prisons at year-end 2013, not 'hundreds of thousands.'

lie: I don't think that [11 million] is an accurate number anymore. I am now hearing it's 30 million, it could be 34 million, which is a much bigger problem.
fallacy: Pants on Fire — Every credible estimate (Department of Homeland Security, Pew, Center for Migration Studies) puts the unauthorized immigrant population at roughly 11 million, with a margin of error of about one million. No researcher has published a number near 30 million.

lie: We have a real unemployment rate that's probably 21%. … Because you have ninety million people that aren't working. Ninety-three million to be exact. If you start adding it up, our real unemployment rate is 42%.
fallacy: Pants on Fire / Falsehood — Even the most expansive alternative unemployment measures top out near 16.4%; the figure appears to conflate the labor-force participation rate (the share of adults not in the labor force, including retirees, students, and stay-at-home parents) with unemployment.

lie: Look, we're the most highly taxed nation in the world — that's why taxes have to go down, business has to come back, jobs have to be back.
fallacy: Falsehood — The U.S. total tax burden was about 26% of GDP in 2014, well below most OECD peers; even on corporate tax rates, the U.S. statutory rate was the highest but its effective rate was not. The U.S. is not 'the most highly taxed nation in the world' on any common measure.

lie: I am the only person on this dais — the only person — that fought very, very hard against us … going into Iraq. … I was so vocal about it. … A delegation was sent to my office to see me because I was so vocal about it.
fallacy: Falsehood / Self-Serving Bias — On September 11, 2002 (six months before the invasion), Trump told Howard Stern he supported invading Iraq ('Yeah, I guess so.'). His earliest known public criticism came in an August 2004 Esquire interview — 17 months after the war began. There is no evidence of a Bush White House delegation to 'silence' him.

lie: You take this little beautiful baby and you pump it with what looks like it's meant for a horse, not a child. … I am totally in favor of vaccines. But I want smaller doses over a longer period of time. … I believe autism will go way down.
fallacy: Pants on Fire / False Cause — Decades of epidemiological research, including CDC studies and the Institute of Medicine, have found no link between vaccines and autism. Spreading out doses beyond the recommended schedule has no demonstrated benefit and increases the window of susceptibility to disease.

lie: The unemployment rate is probably 20 percent, but I will tell you, you have some great economists that will tell you it's a 30, 32. And the highest I've heard so far is 42 percent.
fallacy: Pants on Fire — No recognized economist or government statistic supports a 42% unemployment rate. The figure traces to a column by David Stockman counting retirees, students, stay-at-home parents, and people with disabilities as 'unemployed.'

lie: I watched when the World Trade Center came tumbling down. And I watched in Jersey City, N.J., where thousands and thousands of people were cheering as that building was coming down. Thousands of people were cheering.
fallacy: Pants on Fire / Fabricated Event — Exhaustive searches of contemporary newspaper and broadcast records (including LexisNexis and the AP) found no evidence — and certainly no video — of 'thousands' of New Jersey residents celebrating on 9/11. The closest items were a few uncorroborated rumors, debunked at the time.

lie: [Tweet graphic, 'USA Crime Statistics–2015':] 'Whites killed by whites — 16%. Whites killed by blacks — 81%.'
fallacy: Pants on Fire / False Statistics — FBI data show the opposite of what the graphic claimed: in 2014, about 82% of white homicide victims were killed by whites and about 15% by blacks. The graphic also misrepresented every other racial category, and cited a nonexistent 'Crime Statistics Bureau.'
